SPHERESCAN — Discover What Changes in the Universe

SPHERESCAN is an interactive platform that helps users explore SPHEREx observations and compare astronomical images over time. By visualizing real sky data and observation metadata, it makes infrared astronomy more accessible.

The project enables students, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists to investigate potential changes in the universe through intuitive data visualization, encouraging scientific curiosity and discovery.
summary: SPHERESCAN is an AI-assisted astronomy research prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It analyzes real SPHEREx astronomical observations in FITS format to identify unusual image patterns that may warrant further investigation. The project combines Python, Astropy, image preprocessing, sigma-threshold anomaly detection, multi-epoch image comparison, and PyTorch-based machine learning. By exploring differences between observations and flagging potential anomalies, SPHERESCAN aims to support the investigation of unusual celestial objects and contribute to research related to the Planet X challenge. Its results are preliminary: anomaly candidates require further analysis and scientific validation, and the project does not claim to have detected or confirmed Planet X.
details:
SPHERESCAN: AI-Assisted Anomaly Analysis in SPHEREx Observations

Project Overview

SPHERESCAN is an experimental astronomy research project developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It explores how artificial intelligence and astronomical image analysis can help identify unusual patterns in real SPHEREx observations, with a focus on investigating potential anomalies relevant to the Planet X challenge.

The project does not claim to have discovered Planet X. Instead, it aims to develop a data-driven workflow that can flag unusual observations for further scientific investigation.

How It Works

SPHERESCAN processes astronomical observations stored in FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) format. The project uses real SPHEREx data and Python-based tools to inspect image data, preprocess observations, and search for unusual patterns.

A convolutional autoencoder was trained to learn common image patterns and calculate reconstruction errors. Image regions with unusually high reconstruction errors can be flagged as anomaly candidates. The project also explores statistical sigma-threshold detection and comparisons between observations taken at different epochs.

These methods provide complementary approaches to identifying unusual patterns. Candidate detections require additional checks, including image alignment, instrumental-artifact rejection, coordinate verification, and comparison with other astronomical data.

Technologies and Tools

The project uses Python as its primary programming language, together with:

  • Astropy: Reading astronomical FITS files and working with astronomical data.
  • NumPy and SciPy: Numerical operations and scientific data processing.
  • PyTorch: Building and training the convolutional autoencoder.
  • Scikit-learn: Clustering spatially related anomaly pixels into candidate regions.
  • Streamlit and/or PyQt6: Developing graphical interfaces for exploring observations and analysis results.

The development process also involved examining FITS image extensions, quality flags, variance information, and astronomical coordinates. The machine-learning workflow was evaluated using separate training, validation, and test subsets.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronomical surveys generate large volumes of observational data, making manual inspection alone challenging. SPHERESCAN explores how machine learning and statistical image analysis could help prioritize unusual regions for human review.

The intended benefits include:

  1. Efficient screening: Highlighting image regions that differ from patterns learned by the model.
  2. Reproducible analysis: Using computational methods that can be tested and refined.
  3. Astronomical investigation: Supporting further examination of unusual sources and possible changes between observations.
  4. Accessible research tools: Combining data processing, anomaly scoring, and visualization in a research prototype.

Creativity and Scientific Considerations

The project's creative aspect is its combination of unsupervised anomaly detection with statistical image analysis for astronomical observations. Rather than treating every unusual pixel as a discovery, SPHERESCAN approaches anomalies as candidates that need further investigation.

Important considerations include the quality of the observational data, missing or invalid pixels, instrumental artifacts, background variations, observation alignment, and the risk of false positives. Reconstruction error is an anomaly score, not a probability that an object is Planet X.

SPHERESCAN is an early-stage research prototype. Its results are preliminary, and further validation against known astronomical sources, artifacts, and independent observations is necessary before any candidate can be interpreted as a scientifically confirmed object.

Future Development

Future work could improve multi-epoch image registration, integrate more rigorous source detection and cross-matching, compare candidate regions across additional observations, and evaluate performance against curated astronomical examples. These improvements would help establish whether the approach can reliably distinguish meaningful astronomical anomalies from noise and instrumental effects.

SPHERESCAN demonstrates a practical exploration of AI-assisted astronomical data analysis while maintaining a clear distinction between identifying unusual patterns and confirming a new celestial object.
